summary: A chili-sauce maker's reported AI job cuts spark a national debate days after Beijing told employers to soften AI's hit to jobs, and fingerprints suggest women and teens built the Terracotta Army.
body: Lao Gan Ma, one of China's best-known chili sauce brands, is facing a public backlash over reports that AI replaced most of a production line's workers [^1]. Domestic outlets reported that a senior executive told a business conference that an AI pepper-inspection system cut one line from more than 600 workers to 48 [^1]. The company's HR staff told media on Oct. 26 that he did not mention staffing numbers, but business-registry data show insured employees falling from nearly 3,000 in 2022 to 740 in 2025, though that alone does not prove AI was the cause [^1]. A related Weibo hashtag passed 120 million views; some users called automation normal progress, others called for a boycott [^1]. The story stings partly because the founder, whose face is on every jar, started out as a laid-off worker selling noodles from a street stall [^1].

The timing matters. On Oct. 23 China's State Council, its cabinet, issued guidelines asking officials to monitor AI-related job risks, support re-employment where AI causes "significant disruption," retrain displaced workers, and curb algorithm misuse in hiring [^2]. Sixth Tone reports the guidelines also ask employers in labour-intensive industries to roll out AI cautiously and give advance notice [^1]. My read: Beijing wants fast AI adoption without the social shock, and companies like this one are where those goals collide.

And in archaeology, a study of 79 fingerprints left in the clay of the Terracotta Army, the roughly 8,000 figures guarding China's first emperor's tomb, estimates that about a third came from women and about a fifth from children under 15 [^3]. The authors caution that the method has limits, including a reference database built from European rather than East Asian prints [^3].

reads.summary: How a beloved sauce brand became a test case for AI and jobs in China, and why the evidence for the layoffs is still unclear.
